name: Congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles

clinicalPearls: A congenital, non-progressive restrictive ophthalmoplegia now classified among the congenital cranial dysinnervation disorders rather than a primary muscle disease
Children typically present with bilateral ptosis and eyes fixed in a downgaze position, adopting a compensatory chin-up head posture
Attempted upgaze is severely limited and there may be anomalous convergence or aberrant movements on attempted gaze
Forced duction testing is positive, reflecting secondary fibrosis of the involved muscles
Several genetic subtypes exist; CFEOM1 is linked to KIF21A, CFEOM2 to PHOX2A and CFEOM3 to TUBB3, affecting oculomotor nucleus and nerve development
The primary defect lies in maldevelopment of the oculomotor and trochlear nuclei and nerves, with muscle fibrosis a secondary consequence of chronic denervation
Management focuses on ptosis correction to clear the visual axis and strabismus surgery to improve head posture and alignment
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles is a congenital cranial dysinnervation disorder in which the oculomotor (and sometimes trochlear) nuclei and their nerves develop abnormally. Mutations in genes such as KIF21A and TUBB3 disrupt axon guidance and microtubule-based transport in developing motor neurons, while PHOX2A affects nucleus formation. The resulting aberrant or deficient innervation of the extraocular muscles leads to chronic dysfunction and secondary fibrotic, restrictive change in the muscles themselves. Clinically this produces fixed, restricted eye positions, ptosis and anomalous gaze-evoked movements, with positive forced ductions confirming the mechanical restriction.
additionalInvestigations: Orthoptic assessment of ductions, versions and head posture
MRI of the orbits and brainstem to assess nerves and muscles
Genetic testing including KIF21A, PHOX2A and TUBB3
Assessment for associated cranial nerve or systemic anomalies
redFlags: Acquired or progressive ophthalmoplegia suggesting an alternative neurological or myopathic cause
Amblyopia developing behind a ptotic lid requiring prompt intervention
Associated systemic or brain malformations in syndromic TUBB3 disease
Fatigable ptosis pointing to a myasthenic disorder rather than CFEOM
reference.prognosis: The ophthalmoplegia is stable and non-progressive; surgery can improve head posture, lid position and alignment, but full ocular motility is not restored and binocular function often remains limited.
pitfalls: Mistaking the restrictive picture for an isolated cranial nerve palsy
Neglecting amblyopia treatment while awaiting surgery
Assuming a primary muscle disease and missing the dysinnervation mechanism
Overlooking the familial pattern and not offering genetic counselling
references: Taylor & Hoyt's Paediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
management: No medical cure exists; management is surgical, with staged strabismus surgery using large recessions of the fibrotic, restrictive muscles to improve alignment and reduce the compensatory chin-up head posture
Perform ptosis surgery, usually frontalis suspension, to clear the visual axis, guarding against corneal exposure given poor Bell's phenomenon and defective elevation
Detect and treat amblyopia and correct refractive error to optimise visual development in childhood
Protect the ocular surface with lubrication after lid surgery to prevent exposure keratopathy
Assess for associated cranial nerve or systemic anomalies, especially in TUBB3-related disease
Offer genetic counselling reflecting the KIF21A, PHOX2A and TUBB3 subtypes and their inheritance, and refer to paediatric ophthalmology and clinical genetics
